messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 73
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Journalist
  trauma_type: Man-made disaster
  pcl5: 74

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Visual (Photos): Related photos, Unpredictability: Unpredictable situations, Gustatory (Taste): A specific taste associated with the event
  Maladaptive Strategies: Sit With Back to Wall: always sit with back against a wall to see the room, Compulsive Spending: I spend money impulsively to distract or comfort myself, Freeze When Threatened: freeze completely when feeling threatened
  Threat: Intrusion Monitoring: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home, Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place, Noticing Weapons: I notice potential weapons or dangerous objects in any environment
  Memory: Story Feels Unreal: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me, Memory Replay: My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over., Reliving Event: When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now.
  Negative Appraisals: Thought Avoidance: If I think about the event, I will not be able to handle it, Lost Emotions: I will never be able to feel normal emotions again, Lost Meaning: Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore

Vignette:
Harold was 73 when he first came for help, a divorced journalist who had spent most of his adult life reporting from places where danger was part of the job. In his telling, the event that changed everything was not a natural calamity or an accident but a man-made disaster that had unfolded with brutal speed and intention. He described being on assignment when the scene suddenly became chaotic, people shouting and running, and the ordinary textures of the day were replaced by smoke, noise, and the sound of things breaking. One of the most vivid details he carried was a specific taste in his mouth at the moment of terror, a sharp, chemical taste that had been there while he tried to understand what was happening and what he needed to do next. Even years later, that taste could bring the whole sequence back to him with unsettling immediacy.

At first Harold tried to keep working, telling himself he had seen enough difficult events over the years to understand what had happened and to move on. Instead, the memory began to return with a force that felt less like remembering than being pulled back inside the scene. He said the event was so extreme that, at times, it was hard to believe it had actually happened to him. When the memory came, it did not stay in the past; it played before him like a film that had no pause, and he could be sitting in his apartment, looking at his hands, and then suddenly feel as if he were back there again. What troubled him most was not only that the images recurred but that they arrived with the sensation that it was happening right now. He knew, intellectually, that he was safe in the present, but his body did not always agree.

Certain reminders had become especially potent. Harold avoided related photographs, because a single image could catch him off guard and bring the disaster back with intolerable force. He described seeing a photograph in a newspaper archive and feeling immediately drawn into the old scene, as though the picture had opened a door he could not close. Unpredictable situations were also hard for him; when something happened without warning, even something small, he noticed himself becoming tense and watchful, as if another sudden catastrophe might be about to start. He had also learned to avoid a particular taste associated with the event. If he encountered it in food or drink, he lost his appetite and found himself preoccupied by the memory it carried, so he became careful about what he consumed and where.

Harold’s sense of threat extended well beyond reminders. He said he could not relax even when he knew he was in a safe place, and that after the event he became constantly alert to what might go wrong. At home he listened for sounds that might mean someone was entering, waking at small noises and pausing to distinguish a settling pipe from a step in the hallway. When he went out, he found himself noticing potential weapons or dangerous objects in any environment, scanning tables, counters, and doorways with a habit that felt automatic by now. In restaurants and waiting rooms he always sat with his back to the wall so he could see the room, and if that was not possible he felt uneasy in a way he struggled to explain to others. He also described freezing completely when he felt threatened, a response that left him feeling stuck and exposed rather than able to act.

These reactions had changed the way he moved through daily life. As a journalist, he had once prided himself on curiosity and adaptability, but now he found himself more limited in where he would go and how he would position himself in a room. The smallest unpredictability could leave him scanning for exits and objects he judged unsafe. At times he tried to distract or comfort himself by spending money impulsively, buying things he did not need in the moment, and then later feeling the practical consequences of those choices when the credit card statement arrived. He did not describe this as planned or satisfying; it was more like a quick attempt to get away from the pressure he felt inside, even if only briefly.

Over time he had also come to believe that if he thought too much about the event, he would not be able to handle it. That belief shaped the way he lived with the memory, because he tried to keep it at a distance whenever possible. At the same time, he said he had lost confidence that he would ever feel normal emotions again, and that nothing in his life felt meaningful anymore. These were not abstract statements to him; they were the background tone of his days, especially since retirement and divorce had left him with more quiet and less structure than he once had. By the time he sought help, Harold was tired of living in a state of watchfulness and startled re-experiencing, tired of arranging chairs and scanning rooms and listening at night for sounds at the door. What finally brought him in was the sense that the symptoms had taken over too much of his life, and he wanted relief from the fear that the memory would keep returning as if it were still happening. He was most afraid that it would never stop feeling real, and most hoping that he might one day sit in a room, taste something ordinary, and not be pulled back into that day.
